Again, all of this fallout and barrage of public apologies are a result of a French athlete laughing at a meme of a Chinese dictator who died 50 years ago.

Real Madrid may have stood firm beside Mbappe and freedom of expression, but the unfortunate reality quickly sank in with China ending the broadcast of La Liga matches and the league itself already issuing an apology.

item.title: MATT CALKINS: Why are flagpoles allowed at Portland Thorns games? Alleged attacks raise serious questions
item.description: Ari Laureano says he was struck with flagpoles at a Portland Thorns game after revealing an XX-XY Athletics shirt supporting women's sports.
item.content:encoded:
Ari Laureano is a detransitioned man who sported an XX-XY Athletics T-shirt at a Portland Thorns game Friday. Moments after opening his coat to reveal the logo, he said he was attacked by members of the emphatically pro-trans Thorns crowd.

Laureano said fans struck him twice in the face with flagpoles, then used trans-pride flags to conceal themselves while poking other women in his group — most of whom were holding up a sign reading "Save Women's Sports." And while this unhinged reaction prompts a multitude of questions, one of them has to be: Why do they let attendees bring flagpoles into the stadium?

'SAVE WOMEN’S SPORTS' ACTIVISTS EJECTED FROM NWSL MATCH AFTER BEING STRUCK, CONFRONTED BY PRO-TRANS CROWD'

Most sports venues have strict rules about what fans can bring inside. 

The NBA prohibits poles and sticks, while Major League Baseball stadiums such as Seattle's T-Mobile Park explicitly ban flagpoles. Yet at Providence Park, fans were apparently able to wield objects that, according to Laureano, were used as weapons.

Why is that? Well, spokespeople for the Portland Timbers and Thorns — Providence Park's primary tenants — did not respond to emails inquiring about the policy. The likely explanation is that American soccer clubs have embraced the traditions of their European counterparts, where fans routinely wave flags, sing chants and unfurl massive banners.

But Friday showed the risk associated with allowing said flagpoles into a stadium. And there is no immediate sign that any rule changes are coming.

PORTLAND OFFICIALS SAY CITY DID NOT APPROVE POLICIES THAT LED TO REMOVAL OF WOMEN'S SPORTS SUPPORTERS

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

So what exactly is the policy?

According to the stadium's guest guide, flag and banner poles "must be hollow PVC pipe and no longer than 6' in length." Wooden and metal sticks or poles are prohibited. The guide also says that a flagpole "cannot be used as a projectile, and must not be constructed of wood, metal or other materials that may cause harm to others."

I can't say whether any of the poles Friday violated those specifications. But if Laureano's account is accurate, they were used as weapons regardless of their size or composition.

And that raises a question the Thorns and Timbers should have to answer: Is preserving a soccer tradition worth putting spectators at risk?

item.title: Angel Reese went from taunting Golden State to complaining about officiating as WNBA Finals shifted
item.description: Angel Reese shifted from taunting Golden State to blaming officiating after back-to-back losses put the Atlanta Dream on the brink of elimination.
item.content:encoded:
Following a dominant Game 3 performance in the WNBA Finals, Atlanta Dream forward Angel Reese wanted all the smoke.

After posting 21 points and 12 rebounds in a 97-71 win at State Farm Arena, Reese taunted Golden State players with a "too small" gesture. Atlanta had a 2-1 series lead, and Reese had combined for 51 points and 28 rebounds in consecutive victories.

WNBA PLAYERS, COACHES REFUSE TO EXPLAIN NATIONAL ANTHEM ABSENCES AMID MOUNTING CRITICISM

By the end of Game 3, Reese had become the odds-on betting favorite to win Finals MVP.

Two games later, it’s Reese who looks small.

The 24-year-old forward combined for 15 points on 4-for-20 shooting in Games 4 and 5, both Atlanta losses. She committed nine turnovers, more than twice her four made field goals. What had been a 2-1 series advantage is now a 3-2 deficit, leaving Reese and the Dream one loss from elimination.

WNBA FINALS GAME 6, A POTENTIAL TITLE-CLINCHER, WILL BE HELD IN THE AFTERNOON ON THURSDAY

Her tone has changed, too. After explaining how she was getting into Golden State’s head, Reese is now complaining about the whistle.

During Friday’s media availability before Game 4, Reese sounded like a player who believed she had the Valkyries figured out.

"They’re playing into my mental game where I can take their confidence and just try to do whatever to mess them up," Reese said.

She wasn’t done.

"I’m really confident within myself. Everybody knows that," Reese said.

At the time, she had the performances to back it up. Reese scored 30 points and grabbed 16 rebounds in Game 2, then followed with another double-double in Game 3. Atlanta won those games by a combined 40 points.

Then Reese and Atlanta got a harsh reminder that Golden State reached the WNBA Finals for a reason.

Reese scored eight points on 2-for-12 shooting in Saturday’s 67-62 loss at State Farm Arena. She missed her first five shots of the fourth quarter and committed her sixth turnover on Atlanta’s final possession.

ANGEL REESE'S LATEST WNBA CONTROVERSY SHOWS HOW VICTIMHOOD BECAME CENTRAL TO HER BRAND

Afterward, she acknowledged that her finishing had been a problem.

"I didn’t take my time finishing around the basket like I’ve been doing in the last two games," Reese said.

She added that "it happens" and promised, "I’ll just be better."

But Reese didn't play much better in Game 5.

She finished with seven points on 2-for-8 shooting in Golden State’s 64-55 Game 5 victory at Chase Center. Reese once again had more turnovers (3) than made field goals (2), although she did grab 15 rebounds and dish out five assists.

Before Game 5, Reese drew attention for arriving at Chase Center in a "Protect Black Women" shirt.

After the game, Reese was less interested in saying that she should "be better." Instead, she directed her frustration toward the referees.

"A lot of us are getting fouled, and they’re not calling it," she said.

Reese said the officiating had changed after Atlanta took its 2-1 series lead. She pointed to an uncalled grab by Gabby Williams in Game 4 and complained about being whistled for offensive fouls after defenders pushed her first.

"It definitely took a big turn," Reese said.

Her coach backed her up.

"The contact they allow on Angel compared to everybody else is just ridiculous. Just ridiculous," Karl Smesko said.

Smesko argued that contact on Reese alone should have sent Atlanta to the foul line six to eight more times. He also complained about missed traveling and double-dribble violations, while acknowledging that Atlanta was missing shots it should make.

There were calls worth questioning, including a play in which Veronica Burton’s arm hit Allisha Gray’s head as Gray drove to the basket, knocking off her goggles without a foul call.

But the free-throw numbers hardly tell the story of a series tilted toward Golden State.

Atlanta attempted 31 free throws to Golden State’s 13 in Game 4. The Dream missed nine of them in a five-point loss.

In Game 5, Atlanta again had more attempts, 14-13. Eight of Golden State's 13 free throws came in the fourth quarter, all with the Valkyries leading.

Through five games, Atlanta’s advantage in free throw attempts was 130-78.

WNBA officiating has faced criticism throughout the season, so Reese and Smesko aren’t alone in questioning its consistency.

But no whistle changes Reese’s four made baskets in two games.

Reese won the WNBA’s Defensive Player of the Year award this season. But in these Finals, it’s Kiah Stokes who is looking like the league’s best defender, especially when Reese is trying to score against her.

Stokes has blocked 17 shots through five games, already a WNBA Finals record. She has recorded at least three blocks in every game of the series, and her streak extends to six consecutive playoff games. Stokes tied Lisa Leslie’s 2003 record for the longest such run in a single postseason.

Reese has had 11 of her 59 shot attempts blocked through five games, including eight by Stokes. Those Valkyries blocks account for exactly one-third of Reese’s 33 missed shots.

Golden State’s center followed her 16-rebound, three-block Game 4 with 13 points, eight rebounds and three more blocks Monday. She made three three-pointers in Game 5, one more than Reese’s total field goals.

Across Atlanta’s two losses, Stokes blocked six shots while Reese made four.

Angel Reese was happy to tell Golden State how difficult she was to defend when Atlanta was winning. The Valkyries have since made her prove it, and she hasn’t delivered offensively.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Game 6 is Thursday at 12:30 p.m. ET at State Farm Arena, with Atlanta needing a win to force a deciding game in San Francisco.

Reese wants to be known as one of the best players in the WNBA, and those players are the ones who show up when the spotlight shines brightest.

After Game 3, she was asked about joining the ranks of Atlanta’s sports greats. Reese said she had only been in the city six months, but explained how she measures greatness.

"I think you become one of the greats … when you can win and impact winning," Reese said.

She did that in Games 2 and 3. But her last two performances aren’t going to convince anyone that she belongs in that conversation right now.

item.title: China encroaches dangerously close to US land as a single ship breakdown exposes major vulnerability
item.description: A single mechanical failure on Coast Guard Cutter Healy halved U.S. icebreaking capability as four Chinese research vessels operated near Alaska.
item.content:encoded:
America's ability to maintain a presence in the Arctic remains thin enough that a single mechanical failure cut the Coast Guard's icebreaking capability in the region in half this summer.

And the breakdown comes as Chinese vessels are expanding their activity around Alaska.

Rear Adm. Bob Little, commander of the Coast Guard's Arctic District, told Fox News Digital the failure of Coast Guard Cutter Healy left him with just one of two icebreakers that had been slated to operate in the ice. Meanwhile, four Chinese research vessels were operating in the region.

"Healy's unexpected mechanical failure cut in half my capability to operate up in the ice," Little said.

ARCTIC POWER PLAY GIVES TOP US ADVERSARY NEW OPENING WITH RUSSIA AS US STAKES GROW

The shortfall comes as the U.S. faces a growing need to maintain a presence in waters that can take days to reach. Chinese research vessels are gaining experience in the Arctic and collecting data that can also have military applications, including for submarine operations, while Russia's much larger icebreaker fleet gives Moscow greater ability to move ships and supplies through the region.

The Coast Guard is now racing to add ships, aircraft and surveillance capabilities as shrinking sea ice opens more of the Arctic to navigation. But its next generation of icebreakers is still years away.

"I can't get those icebreakers soon enough, given the operational environment," Little said.

Little said nearly $25 billion in recent funding will support 11 new Arctic Security Cutters, with the first expected to arrive in the region as early as 2028.

The buildup comes as the Coast Guard's operating area is effectively growing. Declining sea ice is opening more navigable water around Alaska, bringing more commercial and military activity into areas that were once harder to reach.

"As that new operational area becomes accessible, we see an increase in human activity for economic development, for military advancement," Little said. "And that activity is creating a need for additional Coast Guard mission."

China has become an increasingly regular presence in those waters. Little said Chinese research activity has grown from as few as one vessel appearing episodically in the Arctic to five last year, while four operated there this year.

Those vessels are not necessarily violating international rules. The Coast Guard Cutter Munro recently returned from a 112-day Arctic patrol that included monitoring Chinese research ships, and Little said the Coast Guard did not observe activity on the surface that fell outside customary law or international norms.

RUSSIA PULLED BACK FROM THE ARCTIC, FOR NOW. NATO MUST ACT BEFORE THOSE TROOPS RETURN

The concern, he said, is what China can learn simply by operating there.

"Any research vessel that operates in the Arctic has the ability to conduct both scientific research," Little said. "It could be economic research that could be for future exploitation of critical minerals and scarce resources."

"And then all of that research helps aid in military activity if you're trying to identify seabed floors and navigate subsurface assets," he added.

Troy Bouffard, director of the Center for Arctic Security and Resilience at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, said China's research activity gives Beijing experience operating in an environment where it has historically had little.

"They're pretty desperate to gain operational experience and knowledge in terms of their growing military capabilities," Bouffard told Fox News Digital.

The research vessels collect legitimate scientific data, he said, but that information can have other applications, "especially when it comes to submarine warfare planning."

For the U.S., Bouffard said the challenge is about more than the number of icebreakers. Unlike the North Atlantic, where the U.S. and its allies have decades of infrastructure and experience, the North Pacific side of the Arctic has far less infrastructure to support a sustained presence.

"If we can't have presence, surface presence in an area, it's very difficult to manage issues that may escalate," Bouffard said.

The distances compound the problem. Getting a ship from Kodiak, Anchorage or Seattle into the Bering Sea can take several days, Bouffard said.

Russia already holds a substantial advantage in its ability to maintain access through its much larger icebreaker fleet.

"Advantage certainly falls in their favor," Little said.

Russia's fleet allows it to maintain access, sea lanes and logistical routes for commercial and military purposes, he said.

"Certainly, as we look at the military advantage, there is a need for the United States to keep up and to ensure that we have ice presence and ice capability," Little said.

The Coast Guard is also watching cooperation between Moscow and Beijing. Little said the service has observed joint Russian-Chinese military surface groups, cooperation between their coast guard forces and Chinese research vessels collaborating with Russia and "likely sharing information."

"Either of them alone are worth paying attention to," Little said. "But anytime they're working together, we're watching closely to see if they pose any threat to homeland security or a military risk to the United States."

item.title: Spain high-speed train crash kills at least 10
item.description: A high-speed RENFE train slammed into a stopped IRYO train in Toledo province, derailing two cars and killing at least 10 people on Wednesday.
item.content:encoded:
A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars and killing at least 10 people on Wednesday in central Spain, authorities said.

Esther Padilla, spokeswoman for the Castilla La Mancha region, said authorities can confirm 10 deaths, but added "that number will surely rise."

It was the second major train accident in Spain this year.

Spain’s rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

CRASH INVOLVING SPEEDING TRAIN, MINIBUS IN BELGIUM LEAVES 4 DEAD INCLUDING 2 CHILDREN

Padilla told state broadcaster TVE that the accident was between two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain. One ran into the tail of the other that had stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track. She said the cause of the crash was not known.

The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left one car shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.

Spanish Health Minister Mónica García told TVE that emergency workers were focusing on rescuing survivors and bodies from the two most damaged train cars. She said that the injured are being sent to different hospitals in the area.

"It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy," García said.

BYSTANDER VIDEO CAPTURES NORFOLK SOUTHERN TRAIN T-BONING SEPTIC TRUCK AT VIRGINIA RAILROAD CROSSING

The accident involved a train from Spain’s state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO. It appeared the RENFE train rammed the IRYO train, Spanish media reported. Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January.

Padilla said that 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.

IRYO, an Italian-owned company, said in a statement that it has "activated its security protocols and is closely working with authorities."

The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, told Spanish state broadcaster TVE that civil protection authorities had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to attend to injured passengers.

A military emergency brigade was deployed to help emergency services, firefighters and police to the crash site.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez cancelled his agenda to focus on the crash. He wrote on X that he was "dismayed by the serious train accident in Toledo."

"Emergency services are working on site to attend to the affected passengers," wrote Sánchez, who faces a national election next month. "All my thoughts are with the victims and their families."

The regional president of Castilla La Mancha, Emiliano García-Page, wrote on X that he was on his way to the crash site.

In January, 45 people died in southern Spain when a train jumped the track and hit an oncoming train. The crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people. The January incident shook the confidence the European country has in its extensive high-speed rail network.

item.title: Weight-loss drug could help address nighttime sleep disruptions for millions
item.description: Eli Lilly's retatrutide cut breathing interruptions and drove significant weight loss in sleep apnea patients, as well as cardiovascular benefits.
item.content:encoded:
An experimental obesity drug significantly reduced breathing interruptions and other symptoms of obstructive sleep disorder in two clinical trials, according to new research published in The New England Journal of Medicine.

Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) affects more than 50 million Americans, and about 80% of cases are undiagnosed, according to the National Sleep Foundation.

The study examined whether retatrutide, an investigational weight-loss drug from Eli Lilly, could help treat OSA in adults who were overweight or obese.

EXPERIMENTAL OBESITY DRUG OUTPERFORMS TRADITIONAL WEIGHT-LOSS TREATMENTS IN EARLY RESEARCH

Retatrutide is being evaluated in phase 3 TRIUMPH trials as a potential treatment for obesity and related metabolic conditions. The drug has not been approved by the FDA.

The FDA has warned that unauthorized versions of retatrutide have been illegally marketed and sold online for weight loss.

The two phase 3 randomized trials included 691 adults with moderate-to-severe sleep apnea and a BMI of at least 27. Participants received once-weekly injections of retatrutide at doses of 4, 9 or 12 milligrams, or a placebo, and were followed for 80 weeks.

The trials included 243 participants without type 2 diabetes and 448 with the condition.

WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY FIGHT 7 SERIOUS HEALTH PROBLEMS BEFORE THE POUNDS EVEN COME OFF

Participants who received retatrutide lost between 12% and nearly 20% of their body weight and experienced significantly fewer breathing interruptions than those who received a placebo.

About 68% of participants experienced more than a 50% improvement in OSA symptoms, regardless of whether they had type 2 diabetes.

The study also found that hypoxic burden — the severity and duration of low-oxygen episodes caused by breathing disruptions during sleep — fell by about 75% among participants without type 2 diabetes and 65% among those with the condition.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The researchers concluded that retatrutide led to significantly greater reductions in AHI (breathing interruptions) than a placebo among adults with OSA who were obese or overweight, regardless of whether they had type 2 diabetes.

The researchers noted that retatrutide’s lack of FDA approval was a limitation, and further studies are needed to determine how the drug may affect long-term cardiovascular outcomes.

Study co-author Dr. Virend Somers, a cardiologist and professor of medicine at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, told Fox News Digital that while the results were expected, he was surprised by the "magnitude of benefit in patients with type 2 diabetes," as well as the significant reduction in sleep apnea.

"This is a very exciting time in treating sleep apnea patients," Somers said.

Sleep apnea is associated with a higher risk of heart attacks, strokes, high blood pressure and atrial fibrillation. In the trial, participants experienced reductions in several cardiovascular risk factors, including systolic blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, systemic inflammation and neck circumference.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"A reduction in these measures would predict whether these patients were at increased cardiovascular risk," Somers told Fox News Digital.

"In diabetics, blood pressure is a key determinant of future cardiovascular risk, and the fact that we were able to reduce it so significantly was both surprising and exciting."

Somers said retatrutide also improved several diabetes-related measures.

In participants without diabetes, insulin levels fell by more than 50%. Among those with type 2 diabetes, 40% progressed from diabetes to prediabetes and another 40% no longer met the criteria for diabetes, according to the researcher.

The improvements were largely linked to weight loss, which can lead to better sleep and reduced sleep-related impairment, he said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"[The participants] reported much improved sleep beyond just the sleep apnea — what we call sleep-related impairment was significantly reduced," Somers said.

The study included participants who were using CPAP and those who were not. Somers said CPAP use generally declined during the study, suggesting that some patients may eventually require less device-based treatment.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Dr. Wendy Troxel, a RAND senior behavioral scientist in Utah who was not involved in the study, noted that OSA is often under-diagnosed and under-treated, especially among postmenopausal women.

"Although CPAP remains the frontline treatment for sleep apnea, my hope is that greater awareness of treatment options may encourage more people to get screened and seek treatment," she told Fox News Digital.

Somers noted that the condition completely resolved in about 25% of participants without diabetes and 15% of those with type 2 diabetes.

The study’s findings do not mean patients should stop using CPAP or other prescribed treatments, the researchers emphasized. Additional research is needed to determine retatrutide's long-term safety and effectiveness for sleep apnea.

"There’s hope on the horizon," Somers said. "We have the CPAP, we have mandibular devices, we have postural therapy, where you try to avoid sleeping on your back, and now we’ve got drug therapies that can potentially not just reduce your apnea, but also make you sleep better ... and reduce the risk of future cardiovascular events."

item.title: Greta Thunberg’s radical turn deserves scrutiny, not applause
item.description: From Paris protests to Gaza flotillas, Greta Thunberg's activist shift raises unanswered questions about funding and ties to extremist movements.
item.content:encoded:
Greta Thunberg recently traveled to France to applaud the protest movement. Wearing a black-and-white scarf associated with pro-Palestinian activism, she appeared outside a high school in a Paris suburb and lent her celebrity to demonstrations marred by rioting, arson and vandalism — with authorities already putting the damage at no less than $34 million. 

Thunberg brought the applause. Taxpayers were left to pay for the destruction.

Her appearance fits a broader pattern of increasingly radical alliances and support for extremism. Before traveling to France, Thunberg had endorsed a motion declaring that "Zionism is racism" adopted by Britain’s Green Party on Oct. 4.

WEAPONIZING THE CHARGE OF GENOCIDE FUELS AN INCREASINGLY DANGEROUS ANTISEMITISM

Her radical turn has been unfolding for years. Yet in progressive circles, she remains the Mother Teresa of the activist left — a secular saint whose moral authority is taken for granted and whose political judgment rarely faces scrutiny.

As a Swede, I watched Thunberg join ABBA, Volvo and IKEA among my country’s most celebrated exports. Political leaders welcomed her. International institutions handed her a microphone. Much of the liberal media mistook her indignation for insight.

She addressed parliaments, collected international prizes and was even touted for the Nobel Peace Prize. The world’s elites welcomed her criticism — and seemed rather pleased to be seen listening. The schoolgirl became a full-time activist and a political force. Her immunity from scrutiny survived the transition.

As Gaza moved to the center of the progressive agenda, the climate movement’s global poster child became an increasingly vocal campaigner against Israel.

Her endorsement of the "Zionism is racism" motion shows how far that shift has gone. Criticizing Israeli government policies is one thing. Denying Jews the right to self-determination is another. The International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism — endorsed by the United States and 42 other countries — lists denying that right, including by depicting Israel’s very existence as racist, among its examples of Jew-hatred.

SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

Her choice of allies raises further questions. In Stockholm, Thunberg accepted an award from the Union of Palestinian Communities and Institutions in Europe — an organization that sent condolences to Hamas following the killing of its leader, Ismail Haniyeh.

The representatives presenting the award wore scarves bearing the emblem of the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine (DFLP), a Marxist-Leninist terrorist organization whose armed wing participated in the Oct. 7 attacks. Those questions followed her to sea. She joined two Gaza-bound missions and was detained and deported by Israel. Israeli authorities accused flotilla organizers of links to Hamas — allegations Thunberg rejected.

Financial disclosures published by the Stockholm-based Greta Thunberg Foundation put its cumulative receipts and donations of award and prize money at approximately $1.3 million as of October 2025. Donations and royalties cover operating expenses, according to the foundation, which states that it does not pay Thunberg.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Meanwhile, her reported personal taxable income for 2024 was roughly $7,000. That figure alone does not explain how her globe-trotting activism is financed. Who pays for her travel, logistics and organizing? Who funds the publicity and campaign machinery behind her activism? Thunberg must answer those questions as readily as she demands answers from governments and corporations.

From France to Gaza, Thunberg increasingly resembles a conflict influencer: confrontation supplies the platform, and indignation over the cause du jour supplies the brand. Whatever the cause, Greta Thunberg takes center stage. It looks less and less like solidarity and more like narcissism dressed as a political cause.

For a conflict influencer, peace and coexistence make poor content. Confrontation keeps the cameras rolling — and Greta in the frame.

Until she answers who funds her campaigns, what she stands for beyond slogans and why she embraces movements shadowed by extremism while preaching morality to democracies, her claim to be a voice of conscience rings hollow.

She is a warning — to my country and to the world.

item.title: Popular Christian YouTuber releases biblical fantasy novel meant to challenge today’s dark content
item.description: Popular Christian YouTuber releases biblical fantasy novel, says Hollywood needs less “Game of Thrones" and more “Narnia"
item.content:encoded:
Bible teacher and popular YouTuber Daniel Maritz is now sharing his take on the battle between light and darkness as the new co-author of the biblical fantasy novel "Lightborn: Dawn of Darkness."

Maritz, who co-wrote the book with his brother Hernu, described the novel as the first in a larger saga centered on a world before the biblical flood, where ancient history and mythology intertwine.

There, the main character — born a slave and named Uldako — seeks to uncover the deeper truths about his world, his heritage and the war behind all wars. He walks a path of survival, pursued by beasts, scorched by loss and drawn toward an ancient prophecy involving the Lightborn.

MEL GIBSON SAYS 'MONSTER' EPIC 'PASSION' SEQUEL SPANS SPIRITUAL REALMS — AND THIS TIME, IT'S IN ENGLISH

If it sounds like a video game, Maritz and his brother would likely agree. In fact, the two also plan to create a companion video game based on the book through their company, Ruach Entertainment.

"Both of which are meant to relate to what’s happening in the world today — in culture, entertainment and basically everything that’s around us," Maritz told Fox News Digital, noting that although the story is ancient, it is still relevant today. "There is not only a battle between light and darkness in Hollywood, but also in education, religion and culture in general."

'WIZARDS OF WAVERLY PLACE' STAR DAVID HENRIE SAYS HIS FAITH COST HIM AGENTS, MONEY AND FRIENDS IN HOLLYWOOD

In a recent Fox News Digital opinion piece, Maritz pointed out that darker content is actually "a distraction from the good of fantasy: the imagined worlds, heroes and adventures that call fans to a higher ethos."

Maritz, who is from South Africa, grew up as the youngest of five children. He has spoken about two of his brothers who died, including one who was murdered in Johannesburg and another who was killed following a car crash.

It was while sitting by his brother Etienne’s side in the hospital that Maritz experienced an awakening of sorts. He recalled hearing a voice ask him, "Daniel, where would you have gone if you died?" That’s when he knew he wanted to create stories for today that look back to the lessons of the Bible in a world oversaturated with violence and darkness.

"So entertainment changes not just the West, but culture as we know it today. And so we have a lot of shows like ‘Game of Thrones' and other shows that bring a lot of vulgar scenes into them and a lot of cussing," Maritz explained.

NETFLIX FACES TURMOIL AS GRETA GERWIG'S $280 MILLION 'NARNIA' MOVIE LOOKS HEADED FOR DISASTER

Maritz modeled his book after works such as C.S. Lewis’ "The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe," which is deeply infused with Christian theology while serving as a rich Christian allegory and J.R.R. Tolkien’s "The Lord of the Rings," which is also rooted in Christian theology.

According to Maritz, today’s society is addicted to entertainment and what he describes as "the evil side of it."

FORMER DISNEY STAR DAVID HENRIE REJECTED 'SECULAR' HOLLYWOOD LIFESTYLE AFTER LIFE-CHANGING MONASTERY VISIT

"It’s through entertainment, through politics and education that they mostly try to change culture as we know it," he said. "And I think people are waking up and getting tired of it — especially when they start changing stories that we know were written by great writers like C.S. Lewis. We know that he wrote the character of Aslan to represent Jesus in this world."

In terms of adapting "Lightborn: Dawn of Darkness" into an interactive experience, Maritz, whose YouTube channels include DLM Christian Lifestyle and DLM Christian Perspective, wants it to serve as an alternative to more violent video games.

SKILLET’S JOHN COOPER SAYS CHRISTIANS WHO CALL ROCK MUSIC ‘DEMONIC’ ARE ‘GETTING THE GOSPEL WRONG’

"We’ve got to share the Gospel because there are 3.5 billion gamers in the world. This industry is bigger than the music and film industries combined. But there’s just darkness in there," Maritz said, noting that many young people use video games as an escape. "Today’s games are just a different form of storytelling, but they let you engage with it."

As he wrote in his Fox News Digital piece, "The question, then, is not whether evil exists, but whether fantasy creators ask their video game players to fight it or practice it, whether fantasy authors craft stories that expose darkness or train an audience to enjoy it."

"To every storyteller reading this: The desire for wonder without wreckage is enormous. We need to craft worlds worth losing ourselves in for an afternoon, with heroes worth following into the dark because we trust they’re going to lead us back into the light," he wrote.

item.title: Inside Melania Trump's secret diplomatic role in the Russia-Ukraine ceasefire deal
item.description: Melania Trump spent weeks negotiating between Moscow and Kyiv to broker a localized ceasefire in Oleshky, a devastated city in Ukraine's Kherson region.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: Moscow and Kyiv remain locked in a yearslong grinding war, but in one Ukrainian city, the fight has quieted — and soon the Russian-occupied aging population in Oleshky will be offered humanitarian relief and a way out.

Behind the localized ceasefire is an unlikely mediator: first lady Melania Trump. And her diplomatic effort in the war-torn region is not over, Fox News Digital has learned.

Trump spent weeks moderating between Russian and Ukrainian officials to hammer out a deal over the devastated city in Ukraine's Kherson region, ultimately winning the trust of both governments to serve as their "exclusive intermediary," according to a senior adviser for the first lady.

The agreement brought officials from both countries together in Belarus last week to sign off on a detailed humanitarian operation aimed at getting food, clean water, medicine and doctors into Oleshky, Ukraine, and providing safe passage out for residents who want to leave.

Fox News Digital obtained the signature pages of the agreement, signed Oct. 23 by Russia's human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, and her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmytro Lubinets. The documents also lay out plans for continued humanitarian operations in the region coordinated with the first lady.

For the Slovenia-born first lady, the war in her native Europe was not entirely unfamiliar territory: she had already mediated exchanges of Ukrainian and Russian children. Negotiating an agreement to stop the fighting, however, marked a significant expansion of that role.

MELANIA TRUMP'S ADVISOR REVEALS HOW SHE BRIDGED PUTIN, ZELENSKYY TO BROKER FRONTLINE UKRAINE TRUCE

Just across the Dnipro from the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson, Oleshky was once home to roughly 24,000 people. Russia seized the city at the outset of its 2022 invasion, and years of occupation and fighting have reduced its population to around 2,000, many of them elderly.

The city now sits squarely on the front line.

Russian forces use Oleshky as a base for attacks across the river into Kherson, while Ukrainian forces target Russian positions in and around the city. Roads have been mined, food and medicine have become scarce and basic services have largely collapsed.

"It's hell there," Yuri Sobolevsky, deputy chairman of the Kherson regional council, told The New York Times. "People need to be evacuated from there, 1,000%. They're living 24/7 under risk of death."

For Ukraine, the humanitarian mission presents a difficult tradeoff. The civilians trapped in Oleshky are Ukrainians in desperate need of food, medicine and a safe route out. But the city remains under Russian occupation and sits on an active front line, meaning halting attacks long enough to reach them also means temporarily easing military pressure on Russian forces operating in the area.

Getting Russia and Ukraine to stop firing at each other has proven extraordinarily difficult — not just for the first lady, but for her husband and his administration, which has spent much of President Donald Trump's second term trying to bring the war to an end.

In Oleshky, however, both sides found a narrow point of agreement.

Oleshky first came onto Trump's radar during United Nations General Assembly week in September, when the city's worsening humanitarian crisis was raised at a Fostering the Future Together event that she hosted.

By then, the first lady had already worked with both governments to reunify 34 Ukrainian and Russian children with their families across six separate efforts, according to her exclusive senior adviser Marc Beckman, building relationships she was able to leverage when she turned her attention to Oleshky.

"The first lady's relationship with both Russia and Ukraine has been, over time, substantial," Beckman told Fox News Digital. "There's a lot of trust, and there's been a lot of success."

Her team first approached Ukraine and asked whether Kyiv would authorize Trump to serve as its "exclusive intermediary" with Russia. Ukraine agreed in a formal letter, Beckman said. Trump's team then approached Moscow, and Putin responded with a letter granting her the same role on Russia's behalf.

From there, Trump began negotiating with the highest levels of government in Russia and Ukraine, with both Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy involved in the talks, Beckman said.

The U.S. side of the negotiating effort was unusually small. Asked how involved the traditional White House national security apparatus was, Beckman said Trump handled the effort. "It's just the first lady," Beckman said.

"The devil is in the details," Beckman said of the negotiations. "There were moments in time where things became complicated."

What began as an effort to get food, water and medicine to a city on the brink of collapse quickly became an extraordinarily detailed negotiation over how to temporarily stop two armies from fighting.

The agreement remains narrowly focused on humanitarian operations in and around Oleshky and does not halt fighting elsewhere in Ukraine, where Russian and Ukrainian forces continue to battle along a sprawling front.

RECOVERING FROM LUNG SURGERY, POPE LEO URGES PUTIN TO AGREE TO CEASEFIRE IN RUSSIAN-HELD UKRAINE CITY

Trump and Beckman worked through maps, roadways and aerial imagery with the two sides, Beckman said. They negotiated what military equipment could enter the area, how civilians would be evacuated and even arranged refrigerated trucks to recover bodies expected to be found along the way.

"We know all of the military equipment that will be brought in," Beckman said. "We even went as far as organizing for refrigerated trucks for the bodies that are going to be there."

"It's going to be a very bad scene," he added. "That's the level of detail that the first lady was involved in."

The negotiations eventually produced a plan mapped out not just by weeks and days, Beckman said, but by the hour.

Russian and Ukrainian officials reconvened in Belarus at 4 a.m. New York time Friday for what was supposed to be a 5 a.m. signing. But negotiations continued for nearly three more hours, with Trump participating by video, before both sides finally agreed to the terms and signed at 7:40 a.m.

The ceasefire was initially slated to begin Oct. 29, but the two sides moved the startup by two days, with the guns falling silent at 4 a.m. Moscow time Tuesday. Its geographic scope was also expanded beyond Oleshky to provide safe passage through the surrounding Kherson region for humanitarian convoys.

"It was almost like momentum clicked," Beckman said.

Russian Gen. Valery Gerasimov, chief of the General Staff, confirmed Russian forces would cease fire along the Kherson axis and facilitate the safe movement of humanitarian convoys into Oleshky.

The humanitarian mission itself will be led by civilians from both countries, keeping Russian and Ukrainian troops apart as aid enters the city and residents are evacuated.

"If the Ukrainian, the Russian militaries were going throughout Oleshky, they would just kill each other," Beckman said.

Four American journalists from Newsmax will also accompany the mission to interview residents and document where they choose to go, providing a record of their decisions as civilians are evacuated from Russian-held territory.

The humanitarian mission is expected to last about one week, with a goal of wrapping up in early November. If more time is needed, Beckman said both sides could negotiate an extension with the first lady again participating in the talks.

The agreement also envisions a role for Trump beyond the immediate Oleshky operation.

Under the terms signed by the two sides, Russia and Ukraine are expected to establish regular humanitarian aid deliveries and repatriation efforts in communities across the Kherson region following the Oleshky mission, with Trump's assistance and coordination.

Those efforts would take place as needed, but at least once a month, according to the agreement.

item.title: Deep in Trump country, a new generation reveals the divide behind Texas' tight Senate race
item.description: Three Texas Tech roommates reveal how abortion rights, oil and gas policy, and cost of living shape their votes in the Paxton-Talarico race.
item.content:encoded:
LUBBOCK, Texas — They share a roof, split the bills and attend the same university. But as Texas' unexpectedly competitive Senate race takes center stage in West Texas, three college roommates have very different ideas about who should shape the state's future.

The students attend Texas Tech University, where they're balancing classes, career ambitions and newfound independence while navigating political differences that extend far beyond their shared apartment.

For Isabella, the election could shape her future career in oil and gas, an industry heavily influenced by government policy. For Kate, women's healthcare and immigration are driving her support for Democrat James Talarico. And for Candy, rising everyday costs and concerns about public education are shaping her vote.

Their differences came into focus as President Donald Trump descended on Lubbock to rally alongside Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton on Tuesday. Across town, Democrat James Talarico was courting voters in a state Republicans have dominated for decades.

TRUMP WON THIS RELIABLY RED STATE BY DOUBLE DIGITS. NOW A DEADLOCKED RACE IS BRINGING HIM BACK

Inside their cozy off-campus apartment, where laptops lie open, notebooks are spread out and favorite snacks are within arm's reach, the three roommates spoke candidly with Fox News Digital about the issues shaping their political views — and how they navigate those differences under one roof.

"I don't think we’ll flip anytime soon," Isabella said of Talarico’s bid to turn Texas blue for the first time in more than three decades.

Kate, who voted for Talarico, sees things differently.

"I think, as a first-time voter, just in general, it's exciting to just feel like you have the ability to make a change," the 19-year-old who hails from Dallas said.

The competing perspectives come as the Texas Senate race has become a razor-thin contest, despite Trump's nearly 14-point victory in the state in 2024.

A Fox News poll conducted in October found Paxton and Talarico tied at 49% among likely voters, underscoring the unusually competitive contest in a state where Republicans have maintained a firm grip on statewide politics since the 1990s.

MEET THE VOTERS WHO COULD BREAK THE GOP’S DECADESLONG GRIP ON A REPUBLICAN STRONGHOLD

For Isabella, the election is closely tied to her career ambitions.

Studying oil and gas at Texas Tech, she said Republican policies offer a more favorable environment for the energy industry, particularly when it comes to pipeline construction and government regulations.

"I don't think that there should be extreme regulations against exploration and production," she said.

Kate, meanwhile, said her support for Talarico was driven largely by his positions on abortion and immigration.

"I think that women should have the right to their own bodies," she said, expressing opposition to Texas' near-total abortion ban.

She also praised Talarico's approach to immigration enforcement, arguing that authorities should prioritize dangerous criminals rather than people working and contributing to their communities.

HIGH PRICES PUT TRUMP’S ECONOMY IN THE SPOTLIGHT AS THE GOP FIGHTS TO HOLD CONGRESS

Candy, 21, who grew up in Chico, Texas, said she voted for Talarico and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa, citing public education, healthcare and affordability.

Candy said filling up her car now costs roughly $60 to $70, nearly double the $30 to $35 she previously paid. For a college student already juggling tuition, groceries and other living expenses, that extra cost every week adds up quickly, leaving less room in her budget.

"That 30 or 40 [dollars] could go toward other expenses," she explained.

Despite supporting Democrats, Candy expressed uncertainty about whether Texas is ready for a broader political shift. "I believe there's hope for Texas, but I don't think Texas is as blue yet," she said.

Kate expressed similar uncertainty, saying her experience in a college town has exposed her to more liberal viewpoints than she might not encounter elsewhere in the state.

"I hope it flips, but I also am not certain that it'd flip, and it wouldn't surprise me if we didn't flip," Kate said.

For Isabella, the prospect of Texas electing a Democrat is considerably less appealing.

But despite their competing political views, the roommates have found common ground in an area that sometimes divides people: their shared living space.

Navigating those differences isn't always easy. Political disagreements occasionally surface, but the students are learning that difficult conversations can offer opportunities to better understand one another without necessarily changing minds.

"I don't think that politics should play a huge role in a friendship or in your living situation," Isabella told Fox News Digital.

Kate expressed a similar sentiment, explaining that she tries to understand her friends as individuals rather than judge them by their political preferences.

"My entire personality doesn't change, based off who I vote for," she said. "And their personality doesn't change based off of who they vote for."
